title: Tiny Snakes Roll Four Times Faster Than They Slither
summary:
Imagine a tiny snake that does not slither away from danger. It rolls. Dwarf reedsnakes in Southeast Asia can roll at about four times their usual slithering speed, and scientists have worked out how they pull off the trick.

Rolling sounds simple, but for an animal it is surprisingly hard. A wheel spins around a fixed axle while the part it carries stays still. An animal has no such trick. If its whole body spins, its head spins too, and that makes balance, steering, and keeping track of direction much harder. The faster the roll, the worse the problem gets.

Dwarf reedsnakes, members of the genus Pseudorabdion, are among the few animals known to roll on purpose to escape predators. The behaviour had been noted in field guides and seen in the field before, but researchers had not fully understood the movements behind it.

To find out, they filmed the snakes from several angles. While rolling, the snakes reached peak speeds of 1.72 to 3.69 metres per second, about four times their fastest slithering speed. Even at that pace, they stayed on a racetrack only 20 centimetres wide, so this is not wild tumbling.

The secret is a carefully timed pattern. Instead of spinning their whole bodies at once, the snakes alternate between rolling on one side and swinging a curved section of the body downward beside the head. Researchers called that downward sweep a stroke. With each cycle, the side touching the ground switches, and the stroke changes direction, left to right, then right to left.

Best of all, the head stays out of the spin. While the rear of the body rotates rapidly, the head points forward at a nearly constant height, like a steady lookout. That control turns a clumsy tumble into a speedy escape.
why_it_matters: It shows how animals can solve a hard movement problem with timing and control, and it helps scientists understand how bodies, balance and steering work in nature.

background_read: Snakes usually move by sliding their bodies along the ground, a movement called slithering.
Animals that hunt them are called predators, and escaping quickly can mean survival.
Rolling is a very different way to move, because a rolling body must keep its balance and direction while it turns.
Researchers study such movements by filming animals from several angles, so they can see exactly how each part of the body moves.
